title: Discrete Mathematics
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned 200L Discrete Mathematics for Computer Science curriculum (set theory, logic, relations and functions, combinatorics, graph theory, Boolean algebra, proof techniques). Content overlaps in topic area with LASU's own CSC204 'Introduction to Discrete Mathematics' course description (set theory, relations, Boolean algebra and lattices, logic, graph theory, matrices), authored here under the assigned code CSC215.

questions.question: In set theory, what is the union of two sets A and B (A ∪ B)?
options: The set of all elements in A, in B, or in both
The set of elements common to both A and B
The set of elements in A but not in B
The set of all possible subsets of A and B
questions.correct_answer: The set of all elements in A, in B, or in both
questions.explanation: The union operation combines all elements that appear in either set, without duplication.

questions.question: What is the cardinality of the power set of a set with n elements?
questions.explanation: The power set contains every possible subset of a set, and a set with n elements has exactly 2^n subsets, including the empty set and the set itself.

questions.question: Two sets A and B are disjoint if:
options: Their intersection is the empty set
Their union equals the universal set
A is a subset of B
questions.correct_answer: Their intersection is the empty set
questions.explanation: Disjoint sets share no common elements, meaning A ∩ B = ∅.

questions.question: In propositional logic, what is the truth value of the conjunction (P ∧ Q) when P is true and Q is false?
options: Depends on the negation of P
questions.correct_answer: False
questions.explanation: The conjunction (AND) is only true when both operands are true; since Q is false here, the whole expression is false.

questions.question: What is the truth value of the disjunction (P ∨ Q) when P is false and Q is true?
questions.correct_answer: True
questions.explanation: The disjunction (OR) is true if at least one operand is true; since Q is true, the whole expression is true.

questions.question: The conditional statement 'P → Q' is false only when:
options: P is true and Q is false
P is false and Q is true
Both P and Q are false
Both P and Q are true
questions.correct_answer: P is true and Q is false
questions.explanation: A conditional (implication) is false only when the hypothesis (P) is true but the conclusion (Q) is false; it is vacuously true whenever P is false.

questions.question: What is the contrapositive of the statement 'If P, then Q'?
options: If not Q, then not P
If not P, then not Q
questions.correct_answer: If not Q, then not P
questions.explanation: The contrapositive of 'P → Q' is '¬Q → ¬P', and it is logically equivalent to the original statement.

questions.question: According to De Morgan's laws, what is the negation of (P ∧ Q)?
questions.correct_answer: ¬P ∨ ¬Q
questions.explanation: De Morgan's law states that ¬(P ∧ Q) is logically equivalent to (¬P ∨ ¬Q).

questions.question: In predicate logic, what does the universal quantifier '∀x P(x)' assert?
options: P(x) is true for every value of x in the domain
P(x) is true for at least one value of x
questions.correct_answer: P(x) is true for every value of x in the domain
questions.explanation: The universal quantifier ∀ ('for all') asserts that the predicate holds for every element in the specified domain.

questions.question: What does the existential quantifier '∃x P(x)' assert?
options: There exists at least one x for which P(x) is true
P(x) is true for all x
No value of x makes P(x) true
questions.correct_answer: There exists at least one x for which P(x) is true
questions.explanation: The existential quantifier ∃ ('there exists') asserts that at least one element in the domain satisfies the predicate.

questions.question: A relation R on a set A is called 'reflexive' if:
options: (a, a) ∈ R for every element a in A
(a, b) ∈ R and (b, c) ∈ R implies (a, c) ∈ R
questions.correct_answer: (a, a) ∈ R for every element a in A
questions.explanation: Reflexivity requires every element to be related to itself.

questions.question: A relation R is called 'symmetric' if:
options: Whenever (a, b) ∈ R, then (b, a) ∈ R also
Every element relates only to itself
(a, b) ∈ R and (b, c) ∈ R implies (a, c) ∈ R
R has exactly one ordered pair
questions.correct_answer: Whenever (a, b) ∈ R, then (b, a) ∈ R also
questions.explanation: Symmetry means that if a is related to b, then b must also be related to a.

questions.question: A relation that is reflexive, symmetric, and transitive is called a(n):
questions.correct_answer: Equivalence relation
questions.explanation: A relation satisfying reflexivity, symmetry, and transitivity is defined as an equivalence relation, and it partitions the set into equivalence classes.

questions.question: What is a 'partition' of a set induced by an equivalence relation?
options: A division of the set into disjoint, non-empty subsets (equivalence classes) whose union is the whole set
A single ordered pair from the relation
A function mapping the set to itself
questions.correct_answer: A division of the set into disjoint, non-empty subsets (equivalence classes) whose union is the whole set
questions.explanation: An equivalence relation partitions its underlying set into disjoint equivalence classes that together cover the entire set.

questions.question: A function f: A → B is called 'injective' (one-to-one) if:
options: Different elements of A always map to different elements of B
Every element of B has a pre-image in A
A and B have the same cardinality
f maps every element of A to a single fixed element of B
questions.correct_answer: Different elements of A always map to different elements of B
questions.explanation: An injective function never maps two distinct inputs to the same output.

questions.question: A function f: A → B is called 'surjective' (onto) if:
options: Every element of B is the image of at least one element of A
Every element of A maps to a unique element of B
A is a subset of B
questions.correct_answer: Every element of B is the image of at least one element of A
questions.explanation: Surjectivity requires the function's range to cover the entire codomain B.

questions.question: A function that is both injective and surjective is called:
questions.correct_answer: Bijective
questions.explanation: A bijective function is a one-to-one correspondence between two sets -- it is both injective and surjective, and therefore invertible.

questions.question: In how many ways can 5 distinct books be arranged on a shelf?
questions.explanation: The number of arrangements (permutations) of 5 distinct items is 5! = 5x4x3x2x1 = 120.

questions.question: How many ways can a committee of 3 people be chosen from a group of 7, where order does not matter?
questions.explanation: This is a combination: C(7,3) = 7! / (3! x 4!) = 35.

questions.question: What is the difference between a permutation and a combination?
options: A permutation considers order, while a combination does not
A combination considers order, while a permutation does not
Permutations apply only to numbers, combinations only to letters
questions.correct_answer: A permutation considers order, while a combination does not
questions.explanation: Permutations count arrangements where order matters, while combinations count selections where order is irrelevant.

questions.question: The Pigeonhole Principle states that if n items are placed into m containers with n > m, then:
options: At least one container must contain more than one item
Each container has exactly one item
The number of items must equal the number of containers
questions.correct_answer: At least one container must contain more than one item
questions.explanation: The Pigeonhole Principle is a basic counting argument: you cannot fit more items than containers into separate containers without at least one container holding more than one item.

questions.question: In graph theory, what is a 'simple graph'?
options: A graph with no loops and no multiple edges between the same pair of vertices
A graph with only one vertex
A graph where every vertex is connected to every other vertex
A graph with weighted edges only
questions.correct_answer: A graph with no loops and no multiple edges between the same pair of vertices
questions.explanation: A simple graph excludes self-loops (edges from a vertex to itself) and parallel/multiple edges between the same vertex pair.

questions.question: What distinguishes a directed graph from an undirected graph?
options: Edges in a directed graph have a specific direction (from one vertex to another)
questions.correct_answer: Edges in a directed graph have a specific direction (from one vertex to another)
questions.explanation: In a directed graph (digraph), each edge is an ordered pair indicating a direction, whereas undirected graph edges have no direction.

questions.question: What is the 'degree' of a vertex in an undirected graph?
options: The number of edges incident to that vertex
The number of vertices in the graph
The shortest path length from that vertex to any other
The total number of edges in the graph
questions.correct_answer: The number of edges incident to that vertex
questions.explanation: A vertex's degree counts how many edges connect to it.

questions.question: According to the Handshaking Lemma, the sum of all vertex degrees in an undirected graph equals:
questions.correct_answer: Twice the number of edges
questions.explanation: Each edge contributes exactly 2 to the total degree count (one for each endpoint), so the sum of degrees is always 2|E|.

questions.question: Two graphs are 'isomorphic' if:
options: There exists a one-to-one correspondence between their vertices that preserves adjacency
They have the same number of vertices only
One graph is a subgraph of the other
questions.correct_answer: There exists a one-to-one correspondence between their vertices that preserves adjacency
questions.explanation: Graph isomorphism means the two graphs are structurally identical -- a bijection between vertex sets exists such that adjacency is preserved.

questions.question: A 'tree' in graph theory is defined as:
options: A connected graph with no cycles
Any graph with exactly one vertex
A graph where every vertex has degree 2
questions.correct_answer: A connected graph with no cycles
questions.explanation: A tree is a connected, acyclic graph; a tree with n vertices always has exactly n-1 edges.

questions.question: In Boolean algebra, what is the result of A AND 1 (A ∧ 1)?
questions.correct_answer: A
questions.explanation: The identity law of Boolean algebra states that A AND 1 always equals A, since 1 is the identity element for AND.

questions.question: What is the result of A OR NOT A (A ∨ ¬A) in Boolean algebra?
questions.correct_answer: 1 (always true)
questions.explanation: This is the law of excluded middle / complement law: a variable ORed with its complement always yields true (1).

questions.question: In lattice theory, what is the 'meet' of two elements typically analogous to?
options: The greatest lower bound (analogous to AND / intersection)
The least upper bound (analogous to OR / union)
questions.correct_answer: The greatest lower bound (analogous to AND / intersection)
questions.explanation: In a lattice, the 'meet' operation gives the greatest lower bound of two elements, mirroring set intersection or logical AND.

questions.question: Which proof technique involves assuming the statement is false and deriving a logical contradiction?
questions.correct_answer: Proof by contradiction
questions.explanation: Proof by contradiction assumes the negation of the statement to be proved, then shows this assumption leads to a logical contradiction, thereby proving the original statement true.

questions.question: What are the two essential steps of a proof by mathematical induction?
options: The base case and the inductive step
questions.correct_answer: The base case and the inductive step
questions.explanation: Induction requires proving the statement holds for a base case (usually n=1 or n=0), then proving that if it holds for n=k, it also holds for n=k+1.

questions.question: What is a matrix in the context of discrete mathematics used to represent a graph called?
questions.correct_answer: An adjacency matrix
questions.explanation: An adjacency matrix is a square matrix where entry (i, j) indicates whether (and possibly how many) edges connect vertex i to vertex j.

questions.question: In an adjacency matrix for an undirected simple graph, what property does the matrix always have?
options: It is always the identity matrix
questions.correct_answer: It is symmetric
questions.explanation: Because edges in an undirected graph have no direction, if vertex i connects to vertex j, then j also connects to i, making the adjacency matrix symmetric about its diagonal.

questions.question: Two positive integers a and b are said to be 'relatively prime' (coprime) if:
options: Their sum is a prime number
questions.correct_answer: Their greatest common divisor (GCD) is 1
questions.explanation: Two integers are coprime when they share no common positive divisor other than 1.

questions.question: What does the modulo operation (a mod n) return?
options: The remainder when a is divided by n
The quotient when a is divided by n
The greatest common divisor of a and n
The product of a and n
questions.correct_answer: The remainder when a is divided by n
questions.explanation: The modulo operation gives the remainder of integer division, which is fundamental in discrete mathematics and computer science (e.g., hashing, cryptography).
